method: One visual/manual reading of each printed page; handwriting ignored; claims are captured as printed and are not yet accepted as corrected facts.

facts: Tungsten is stated to be obtained from wolframite.
The printed melting point of tungsten is 3422 degrees Celsius.
Tungsten is stated to be used as an electric-bulb filament.
The page states that about 95 percent of tungsten use is connected with steel and military or high-strength applications.
Ferro-tungsten containing up to 75 percent tungsten is linked with military equipment, cutting tools, construction and metal-working equipment.
Indian tungsten occurrences are listed in Karnataka, Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra and West Bengal.
Andhra Pradesh occurrences are printed at Kangundi in Chittoor and Ramachandrapuram in Konaseema district.
Degana in Rajasthan and a locality printed as Chandrapur in West Bengal are identified as production locations.
Mica is presented as a mineral family extending from muscovite or potash mica through phlogopite or magnesium mica to biotite or iron-magnesium mica.
Micas are described as hydrous silicates that split into thin sheets.
Mica uses listed are plastics, drilling fluids, polymers, paints, cosmetics, medicines and the electrical industry.
Printed mica resources are 6.35 lakh tonnes.
Printed mica resource shares are Andhra Pradesh 41 percent, Rajasthan 28 percent and Odisha 20 percent, with Maharashtra and Bihar also listed.
Gudur, Nellore and Atmakur are listed as Andhra Pradesh mica locations.
The page says India formerly supplied about 60 percent of world mica and that about 95 percent of present Indian production comes from Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan, Jharkhand and Bihar.
Printed limestone-use shares are 75 percent for cement and 16 percent for iron and steel.
Printed limestone resource shares are Karnataka 27 percent, Andhra Pradesh 12 percent, Rajasthan 12 percent, Gujarat 10 percent, Meghalaya 9 percent and Telangana 8 percent.
Andhra Pradesh limestone locations listed are Betamcherla, Koilkuntla, Dhone, Jammalamadugu, Mydukur and Palnadu.
Printed limestone production shares are Rajasthan 20 percent, Madhya Pradesh 13 percent, Andhra Pradesh 13 percent, Chhattisgarh 11 percent, Karnataka 9 percent and Telangana 8 percent.
The page prints 807 limestone mines, divided into 26 public-sector and 781 private-sector mines.
Marble is described as a rock derived from limestone.
Printed marble resource shares are Rajasthan 63 percent, Jammu and Kashmir 21 percent, Gujarat 6 percent and Chhattisgarh 4 percent, with Madhya Pradesh also listed.
Rajasthan, Gujarat, Jammu and Kashmir, Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh are listed as major marble producers.
Italy, Greece and Spain are named for world marble, and Carrara marble is specifically mentioned.
The page defines dolomite using printed magnesium thresholds of 10 percent and more than 45 percent.
Printed dolomite-use shares are 90 percent for steel and 4 percent for fertilizer.
correction_flags: All resource, production and mine-count values require year labels and current authoritative verification.
The printed dolomite magnesium thresholds appear chemically confused and must be corrected against IBM or GSI definitions.
The tungsten use sentence and the printed West Bengal production locality are unclear and require source verification.
Current district names must not be projected backward without a time label.

facts: Dolomite deposits are listed in Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Karnataka.
Kurnool, Anantapur and Kadapa are listed as Andhra Pradesh dolomite locations.
Odisha, Chhattisgarh and Andhra Pradesh are listed as dolomite-producing states.
Granite is described as containing feldspar, hornblende, pyroxene, quartz and iron oxides and as having a granular plutonic character.
Granite reserves or deposits are listed in Karnataka, Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Gujarat and Andhra Pradesh.
Granite production is listed in Karnataka, Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Gujarat.
Barytes is presented as a heavy mineral associated with barium and sulphur chemistry.
The printed barytes-use sentence mentions medicine, drilling mud and the gas industry, but also appears to confuse barytes with beryllium.
The page assigns 90 percent of Indian barytes deposits to Andhra Pradesh.
Mangampeta and Cheemalapenta in Annamayya district are listed as barytes locations, with Rajasthan, Karnataka and Telangana also named.
The page assigns 95 percent of barytes production to Andhra Pradesh and also mentions Nellore.
A printed Mangampeta deposit figure of 66 million tonnes below a depth of 30 metres is given.
Rajasthan is placed after Andhra Pradesh in barytes production.
Gypsum is linked with fertilizer use.
Rajasthan is assigned 90 percent in the printed gypsum distribution or production statement, followed by Jammu and Kashmir, Tamil Nadu and Gujarat.
Asbestos is described as a fibrous silicate used for fire-resistant clothing, rope and materials.
The page recognizes asbestos as a health hazard and states broadly that it has been banned worldwide.
Asbestos deposits are listed in Rajasthan, Pulivendula in Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka, and the page states that India currently has no production.
Coal is introduced as India's largest mineral fuel resource in the printed account.
The page prints India as fifth in coal reserves and second in coal production.
Printed coal-use shares include 34 percent thermal power, 20 percent iron and steel, 12 percent cement and fertilizer and 11 percent rail transport.
The page prints a coal-bearing or reserve area of 6 lakh square kilometres, calls coal a bridge fuel and black gold, and gives world reserves as 800 to 900 billion tonnes.
structured_records: Granite composition, deposit and producer lists
Asbestos uses, deposits and production statement
correction_flags: Barite is barium sulfate; the apparent barytes-beryllium conflation is a factual error.
The claim that asbestos is banned worldwide is overbroad and must be replaced with jurisdiction-specific and health-risk wording.
Coal ranks, shares, reserve area and world-reserve totals are date-sensitive and require authoritative year-tagged sources.
Granite mineral composition varies and should not be presented as a fixed universal recipe.

facts: The page dates the first Indian coal mine at Raniganj to 1774 and connects it with Warren Hastings, Sumner and Heatly.
Coal India Limited is stated to conduct production through seven subsidiary companies.
Singareni Collieries is described as jointly owned by the central and Telangana governments.
The page prints a claim that India holds 53 percent of world thermal coal, which requires correction.
A GSI reserve figure of 321.34 million tonnes down to 1200 metres is printed; the unit appears erroneous.

Printed state reserve shares are Jharkhand 26.16, Odisha 24.52, Chhattisgarh 17.98, West Bengal 10.05, Madhya Pradesh 8.78, Telangana 6.81, Maharashtra 3.89, Bihar 0.56, Andhra Pradesh 0.50 and Uttar Pradesh 0.32 percent.
Printed state production shares are Odisha 24, Chhattisgarh 21, Jharkhand 19, Madhya Pradesh 16, Telangana 8, Maharashtra 7 and West Bengal 4 percent.
Jharkhand coalfields listed include fields in Dumka, Hazaribagh and Dhanbad, with Jharia called the Ruhr of India and Rajmahal also named.
Odisha coal areas listed include Dhenkanal, Sambalpur, Sundargarh and Talcher.
Chhattisgarh coalfields listed are Korba, Chirimiri, Rampur, Lakhanpur and Jhilimili or Surajpur.
West Bengal coal areas listed include Raniganj, Bardhaman, Bankura and Purulia, with coking and steam coal mentioned.
Madhya Pradesh coal areas listed are Singrauli, Umaria and Pench-Kanhan-Tawa.
Telangana coal areas listed are Jayashankar Bhupalpally, Bhadradri Kothagudem, Komaram Bheem, Mancherial and Peddapalli.
The page prints a coal occurrence in West Godavari, Andhra Pradesh, with an unclear preceding locality name.
Anthracite is printed as hard coal with 80 to 95 percent carbon, highest quality and high calorific value, and is located in Jammu and Kashmir.
Bituminous coal is printed with 40 to 80 percent carbon, black to dark-brown colour, iron-industry use and occurrence in Jharkhand, Odisha, West Bengal, Chhattisgarh and Madhya Pradesh.
Bituminous coal is stated to be India's most abundant coal rank.
Lignite is introduced with a printed carbon range of 40 to 50 percent and moisture of about 35 percent; its account continues on page 451.
structured_records: Yellow table: state-wise coal reserve shares, ten rows
Yellow table: state-wise coal production shares, seven rows
visuals: Two-column yellow comparison table of coal reserves and production by state
correction_flags: The 321.34 figure likely requires billion tonnes rather than million tonnes and must be checked for the reference year.
The 53-percent world thermal-coal claim is implausible and requires correction.
The heading Carboniferous coalfields is geologically unsuitable for a combined list of Indian Gondwana and other coalfields.
All state shares require a reference year; the Andhra Pradesh locality text is unclear.
Coal-rank carbon ranges vary by classification and need authoritative framing.

facts: The lignite account continues by saying it is used substantially for thermal electricity generation.
Lignite areas are listed in Tamil Nadu at Neyveli, Pondicherry or Puducherry, Kerala, Gujarat, Rajasthan and Jammu and Kashmir.
The page states that 52 percent of lignite resources occur at Neyveli in Cuddalore district, Tamil Nadu.
A national lignite resource figure of 44.70 billion tonnes is printed.
Cannel coal is printed with about 40 percent carbon, gas and tar content and the alternative name gas coal.
Peat is printed with less than 40 percent carbon, black colour, and occurrences in the Nilgiris, the Jhelum valley in Jammu and Kashmir, and West Bengal.
Gondwana coal is dated to about 250 million years and is said to contain 98 percent of India's coal resources and 99 percent of production.
The page prints 113 Gondwana coalfields over 80 coal belts.
Gondwana coal regions listed are Damodar, Mahanadi, Son, Godavari, Wardha, Indravati and Narmada valleys or basins.
Tertiary coal is dated to 15 to 60 million years and is located in Assam, Meghalaya, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, West Bengal's Darjeeling area and Jammu and Kashmir.
Graphite is described as an allotrope of carbon and as having a pencil-related use.
Printed graphite resource shares are Arunachal Pradesh 37 percent, Jammu and Kashmir 32 percent, Odisha 10 percent, Jharkhand 9 percent and Tamil Nadu 4 percent.
Printed graphite production shares are Odisha 59 percent, Jharkhand 40 percent and Kerala 1 percent.
Petroleum is described as a hydrocarbon mixture found in impermeable rock traps in marine and coastal sedimentary settings.

Printed world petroleum reserve shares are Middle East 56 percent, North America 16 percent, Africa 9 percent, Central and South America 8 percent, Europe and Eurasia 7 percent and Asia-Pacific 4 percent.
Printed country reserve shares are Venezuela 17, Saudi Arabia 15, Iran 12, Canada 9 and Iraq 8 percent, with India placed 23rd at 0.28 percent.

Printed world petroleum production regions are the Middle East, North America, Europe and Eurasia, Asia-Pacific and South America; listed producing countries are the United States, Saudi Arabia, Russia, Canada and China.
The page states that ONGC was formed in 1956 and began exploration in stages.
The page states that Indian Oil Company was formed in 1981 by combining Burma Oil Company and two government entities; this chronology and naming require correction.
IOC is stated to have expanded exploration from eastern India to the Mahanadi basin and to Rajasthan and the Andaman region.
The page begins a crude-oil reserve statement of roughly one billion cubic kilometres or an equivalent unit, but the sentence continues on page 452.
structured_records: Coal-rank continuation: lignite, cannel and peat
Gondwana versus Tertiary coal age and occurrence list
correction_flags: Gondwana percentages, counts and lignite totals require a dated Ministry of Coal or GSI source.
The graphite shares and all petroleum reserve and production rankings are date-sensitive.
The 1981 Indian Oil formation account appears historically wrong: Indian Oil Company and Indian Refineries were merged into Indian Oil Corporation in 1964.
The crude-oil reserve unit is unclear and the sentence is incomplete on this page.
Peat and cannel carbon ranges require authoritative classification.

facts: The continued crude-oil statement prints 621 million tonnes of reserves, divided as 55 percent onshore and 45 percent offshore.
Oil-bearing states or regions listed are Maharashtra or Western Offshore, Assam, Rajasthan, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Arunachal Pradesh.
The same states are listed in a printed crude-oil production ranking, with Reliance Petroleum and Indian Oil Corporation named as major refining companies.
Mumbai High is stated to lie about 176 kilometres from Mumbai and to have begun ONGC production in 1974.
Mumbai High is described as a 1400 square kilometre S-shaped oilfield.
Gujarat oilfields listed are Ankleshwar, Kosamba, Kalol, Mehsana, Navagam, Lunej and Dholka.
The first offshore petroleum mining in Gujarat is attributed to Aliabet in the Gulf of Khambhat, about 47 kilometres from Bhavnagar.
Rajasthan oilfields listed are Mangala, Bhagyam and Aishwarya in Barmer district.
Assam oil history is traced to Digboi: discovery before 1889, regular production from 1889, and refinery production from 1891.
Other Assam oilfields listed include Hoollong or a similarly printed name, Moran, Naharkatiya, Sibsagar, Rudrasagar, Chandrapur and Lakwa.
Tripura and Cachar or nearby Assam areas are said to have shale-oil occurrences.
Krishna-Godavari Basin oil and gas areas listed include Ravva in Konaseema district and Narsapur in West Godavari district.
The page states that Reliance has major oil and gas reserves in Krishna-Godavari Basin areas.
Tamil Nadu oilfields listed include Narimanam and Kovilappal or Kovilkalappal, with exploration also named in Andhra Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, Rajasthan, Malabar and the Konkan coast.
Arunachal Pradesh oilfields listed are Kharsang, Manabhum, Kumchai and Ningru.
A boxed APPSC Group-I 2022 PYQ asks which of Digboi, Moran, Kalol and Naharkatiya are in Assam; the printed keyed option is 2, corresponding to I, II and IV.
Natural gas reserves are printed as 1380 billion cubic metres, split 64 percent offshore and 36 percent onshore.
The natural-gas field list begins with Western Offshore locations including Mumbai High, Bassein and Neelam, and continues on the next page.
structured_records: Onshore versus offshore crude-oil reserve split
State crude-oil occurrence and production lists
Onshore versus offshore natural-gas reserve split
correction_flags: All reserve totals and onshore-offshore shares require the reference year and authoritative MoPNG or DGH data.
Mumbai High discovery, production-start date, distance and area should be checked against ONGC sources.
Several locality spellings are unclear in print and need gazetteer or DGH verification before publication.
The claim of first offshore mining at Aliabet requires historical verification.
The PYQ should retain its exam identity; its official key must be checked before scored use.
